title: Labour's Bev Craig elected new mayor of Greater Manchester
description: In the first round, Craig secured 47% of the vote, compared with Astley's 21%.This meant the ballot papers from voters who did not select either of th
body: In the first round, Craig secured 47% of the vote, compared with Astley's 21%.This meant the ballot papers from voters who did not select either of them as their first choice were brought back into play.They were checked to see if the second-preference votes were for either the Labour or Reform candidate.They were then added to the first-preference votes.Craig expanded her already significant lead.More than two million people across Greater Manchester's 10 boroughs were eligible to vote in the contest but turnout was just under 25%.Analysis of the votes showed that Craig came top of the poll in the first round of voting in all the 10 local authority areas that make up Greater Manchester.Astley came second in eight of the 10 areas, while the Green candidate Geraldine Coggins came second in Manchester and the Conservative candidate Phil Eckersley was second in Trafford.In her speech, Craig said: "For too many people across our region, life is simply too hard. The generational belief that we had, that if you work hard and do the right thing, your life will be better and the life of the community will be better, is something that many people just don't feel at the minute."She continued: "Everyone deserves a quality home in a good neighbourhood," said Craig, adding that people should be able to plan for their future and for that of their children.She added: "We have to move away from divisive politics, and we'll do it together."Congratulations came from Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell, the MP for Manchester Central, who posted on X, external: "Huge congratulations to @bevcraig our fantastic new Mayor of Greater Manchester."Thank you to our tireless activists who have worked so hard to help deliver this win."

schema.headline: Labour's Bev Craig elected new mayor of Greater Manchester

title: Nancy Guthrie ransom notes released in latest police bid to find kidnappers
description: Police in Arizona have released two ransom notes in the hope the public can help identify whoever abducted the mother of US news presenter Savannah Gu
body: Police in Arizona have released two ransom notes in the hope the public can help identify whoever abducted the mother of US news presenter Savannah Guthrie.The first note, which is treated as apparently credible, demanded millions of dollars in Bitcoin. The other claimed Nancy Guthrie died shortly after she was abducted from her home near Tucson six months ago.The Pima County Sheriff's Office say they cannot verify her death, and the investigation remains active.Officials released the two notes on Friday, asking the public for help identifying the writer, whose "distinct linguistic characteristics may be recognisable".Investigators believe that Nancy Guthrie, who was aged 84 when she was last seen on 31 January, was taken against her will from her home, but they have not shared a possible motive or arrested a suspect.The notes were addressed to Savannah Guthrie and the Guthrie family, and sent to a local TV station in Tucson, Arizona, in the days after Nancy Guthrie disappeared, according to the sheriff. "A friend, family member, coworker, classmate, or acquaintance may recognise these patterns of expression and possess information that could help identify the individual responsible," the sheriff's office said in a statement.The first note, which was received on 2 February, began: "Hello Savannah, we have your mother Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of 7 days. You will need to send bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD before 5PM on Thursday the 5th."If payment is not received, the ransom will be increased to 6 million USD which will need to be paid by 5PM on Monday the 9th. Once payment is received to the bitcoin address below she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop off location back in Tucson. If payment is not recieved [sic] by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5PM, she will be killed."Your mother is aware of this and her life is in your hands. It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible. "You will not be able to contact me from here on out, there will be no negotiation. Do not play games, law enforcement will not be able to help you," the note continued.After what appears to be a redacted sentence, it ends: "She had a white smart watch on the floor of the foot of her bed and the white flood light in backyard was destroyed."Nancy Guthrie, who was taking daily medication, vanished after relatives dropped her off at her home on the evening of Saturday 31 January.Police were contacted when she failed to show up the following morning at a friend's house to watch a virtual Sunday church service.Four days after the first note, the second arrived: "Guthrie Family, we did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention."She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related. She is buried in nature now."Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry."After the second note, Savannah Guthrie - one of the most famous TV presenters in the US - took to Instagram on 7 February to respond."We received your message and we understand," Guthrie said at the time. "We beg you now to return our mother to us... This is very valuable to us, and we will pay."Earlier this week, Guthrie again released a video calling for the kidnappers to "do the right thing" and reveal the location of her mother.

schema.headline: Nancy Guthrie ransom notes released in latest police bid to find kidnappers

title: Spain's PM blames traffickers after 60,000 migrants reach Ceuta from Morocco
description: Spain's prime minister has blamed trafficking gangs after about 60,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco.
body: Spain's prime minister has blamed trafficking gangs after about 60,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco. At least 57 people died during the surge, according to local media.Pedro Sánchez called the incident a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity". Italy has responded by suspending the EU's border-free Schengen arrangements with Spain.The influx comes after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla, another Spanish enclave, cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.As of Friday evening, more than 48,000 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco, Spanish officials said.One man told Reuters news agency he was going back, adding: "It's not good at all, and it's not fun either. I mean, people are dying here. I beg you, please, if you haven't come yet, don't come. Don't do it."Ceuta on the North African coast is separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar. It has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe. During the summer months there is often a big push to reach Ceuta, typically organised over social media.Coveted by Morocco, Ceuta and another Spanish enclave Melilla have long been a flashpoint in diplomatic relations between the two countries. They form the European Union's only land borders with Africa.Local officials had appealed to Madrid for help after a recent rise in attempted crossings, but there were chaotic scenes on Thursday as border controls apparently broke down.Carmen Gonzalez Bermudez who was in the city to see her parents told the BBC that the past day had been "very overwhelming".She said she saw "thousands and thousands of people in swimming costumes and all wet, just coming from the sea", adding that "I know most of them are nice people just looking for a better future for themselves. But we cannot give that to them".Víctor Ortiz Sotomayor told the BBC he had "never seen anything like it", describing the city as "packed with immigrants, in every square and street, mainly looking for food"."There were only a few stores open, but in the end the police advised them to close because of the overwhelming influx of people," he added."My friends, my family and I are all staying at home. We haven't gone outside because we're scared."Referring to a previous surge of migrants into Ceuta, Carmen Gonzalez Bermudez said: "In 2021, we saw our police and our military doing something. Yesterday, they were in the streets, but they weren't doing nothing. So that for starters feels really scary."Ceuta's President Juan Jesús Vivas said the arrivals amounted to around 70% of the city's population - which sits at around 83,600 according to the latest local figures. Spain's Interior Ministry told the BBC that its estimates were slightly lower, citing 50,000 arrivals since the early hours of Thursday.Spain has now deployed its armed forces to bolster security in Ceuta and at its sister city of Melilla, where between 300 to 400 crossings were also reported overnight.Speaking on Friday during a visit to Ceuta, Sánchez said the surge was caused by criminal networks purposefully misinterpreting the recent Supreme Court ruling."What has emerged from our talks with Moroccan authorities is that trafficking mafias took a self-serving interpretation of a Supreme Court ruling" which "spread like wildfire", he said.He added that the government would look at reinforcing the border with Morocco, and that Moroccan authorities were co-operating with the return of those who had entered illegally.Most of those entering Ceuta have been young men, although there are also women and children in the crowds and even babies. Officials estimate that at least 7,000 of those who crossed illegally into the territory in the last 24 hours are minors.Usually, to try to enter Ceuta, migrants swim several kilometres from further up the coast. This time they appear to have been able to get close to the border fence itself with ease. At the start, some even walked along the rocks on the jetty and around the end of it, but most had to swim out and around to reach the beaches on the other side.It's not clear where the Moroccan border guards were at this point and why the groups of migrants were not dispersed or stopped.Morocco, which has a high unemployment rate, witnessed several Gen Z anti-government protests last year - with young people demanding better opportunities and improvements to public services.BBC Verify has looked into migration data released by the UN, external, which reported 2,826 people had crossed into Ceuta up until 15 July this year with another 181 entering via Melilla.The number of migrants crossing into these two territories was already high compared with recent years, which saw 994 migrants enter in 2025, 476 in 2024 and 467 in 2023.Italy's right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the images from Ceuta as "shocking", writing on social media that such "uncontrolled immigration" was a security threat to Europe.Later on Friday Italy suspended the Schengen zone agreement with Spain on free movement. Since the two countries don't have a land border this would only apply, effectively, to flights - which appears simply to mean extra checks for passengers.The Spanish foreign minister said such remarks were "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery". He also summoned the Italian ambassador to Madrid on Friday.Czech Republic's Andrej Babiš also called for the temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership.Responding on X, Sánchez said: "Solidarity and empathy are optional. Respect for European treaties and data is not."US President Donald Trump meanwhile called the situation in Ceuta a "catastrophe" and blamed it on "weak law, bad management". EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the images out of Ceuta were "unacceptable" and must "stop immediately".Finland's Interior Minister Mari Rantanen backed Meloni and said Spain had failed to protect its border, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz demanded Morocco "take back illegal migrants immediately".The Schengen Area is a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have officially abolished controls at their common borders.Additional reporting by Tamara Kovacevic, BBC Verify, Basma El Atti, BBC Focus, Isabella Bull, BBC World Service, and Marina Costa

schema.headline: Spain's PM blames traffickers after 60,000 migrants reach Ceuta from Morocco

title: Greyhounds bound for Australia as New Zealand racing ban takes effect
description: At least two chartered flights carrying up to 150 greyhounds are set to fly to Australia's eastern states, as a New Zealand ban on the sport comes int
body: At least two chartered flights carrying up to 150 greyhounds are set to fly to Australia's eastern states, as a New Zealand ban on the sport comes into effect.Several greyhound trainers in New Zealand are responding to a new ban by moving their dogs to Australia with plans to continue in the sport, governing body Greyhound Racing New Zealand (GRNZ) told the BBC.While the ban across New Zealand takes effect on Saturday, the practice remains legal almost everywhere in Australia.The ban was first announced in December 2024, and legislated in April. Approximately 1,400 greyhounds will retire in New Zealand under the ban and require rehoming.Australian authorities say that greyhounds arriving from New Zealand are classed as "companion animals" which will undergo screening for diseases such as rabies."Australia's import requirements for dogs are based on biosecurity risk, not the intended use of the animal," Australia's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry told a Senate inquiry in June.A spokesperson for New Zealand's Racing Minister Winston Peters called the plans to relocate the dogs "the last gasp actions of a dying industry". Peters said the dog racing industry had "lost its social licence" after multiple reviews concluded that dog and injury death rates "remain unacceptably high", a conclusion that GRNZ disputed.In a statement, a spokesperson for Peters said: "We understand a small number of dogs are being exported to Australia, but the vast majority (1,300 to 1,400) will be rehomed over the next couple of years." "This is a one-off final act rather than an ongoing issue," the spokesperson added.GRNZ Edward Rennell chief executive told the BBC that between six and 10 trainers have expressed interest in relocating to Australia, with most New Zealand citizens not requiring a special visa to live in Australia. Details would be finalised "over the next two weeks", he said.Rennell said "the details aren't locked in" but that his organisation would cover the full cost of the flights, while other costs would be borne by owners and trainers."We will be supporting people that are looking to transfer over," Rennell said.He said some of the dogs will continue training and racing in Australia, although he noted they are likely to be less competitive in professional racing because breeding has largely paused in New Zealand since the ban was announced 18 months ago.Kiwis are still able to bet on Australian greyhound racing, which has a larger commercial presence.Queensland, New South Wales (NSW) and Victoria's industries were collectively worth almost A$2bn (£1.04bn; $1.4m) in 2022-23, which dwarfed New Zealand's $147m total, according to the latest figures published by Greyhounds Australasia.The dedicated body overseeing the closure of the industry in New Zealand, the Greyhound Transition Agency told the BBC: "We understand that arrangements are being made to relocate some dogs to Australia for racing purposes. "However, we are not in a position to comment further on these arrangements."New Zealand announced the greyhound racing ban following three independent reviews into the sport in 2013, 2017 and 2021."We acknowledge the industry made advances in safety, but the high injury and death rates persisted with no sign of improvement," Peters's spokesperson added.In response, Rennell told the BBC: "I will go to my grave saying that the greyhound welfare standards are the best of any racing code in New Zealand."GRNZ has eyed kennels across eastern Australia as destinations for New Zealand's racing dogs.A spokesperson for the Queensland Racing Integrity Commission said the agency "has been advised by Greyhound Racing New Zealand of the arrival of racing greyhounds and the potential relocation of industry participants from New Zealand into Queensland".NSW and Victorian officials said they were not aware of specific relocation plans within their states, noting that greyhounds are permitted to travel across jurisdictions in Australia in New Zealand.Australia's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry did not respond to a request to make further comment.Dozens of greyhounds were also found to have been moved to Australia after New Zealand's ban was first announced.Officials have confirmed 80 greyhounds were exported from New Zealand to Queensland through a chartered flight in April 2025.One trainer and his family were drawn to the "shining lights of the new facility" west of Brisbane, Simon Stout from Greyhounds Australasia told a parliamentary committee hearing in Tasmania on Wednesday.But one federal senator, Mehreen Faruqi of the Greens, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned about loopholes that allow the continued export of racing dogs to this country that neither New Zealand nor Australia seem to care about". Director of the Coalition for the Protection of Greyhounds Kylie Field said Australia already struggles to find residential homes for thousands of retired racing dogs, including 4,100 in NSW."In an attempt to solve the rehoming crisis, the racing industry had devised a program of sending retired greyhounds to the US and Canada," Field said."More than 2,000 dogs have been sent overseas so far." Dog racing is banned in the Australian Capital Territory and Tasmania has announced plans to phase it out.Scotland and Wales both passed legislation outlawing commercial dog racing this year. Most US states have imposed a ban, leaving two racing tracks in West Virginia as the last active operations.

schema.headline: Greyhounds bound for Australia as New Zealand racing ban takes effect

title: Snapchat joins other platforms in the fight against 'AI slop'
description: Snapchat has joined the likes of YouTube, LinkedIn and Substack in a growing effort  to combat fake writing, images and videos that are entirely creat
body: Snapchat has joined the likes of YouTube, LinkedIn and Substack in a growing effort  to combat fake writing, images and videos that are entirely created by artificial intelligence (AI) tools.Such content, commonly called "AI slop", has proliferated online as the tech industry has raced to create a greater number of easier to use generative AI tools that can create anything from essays to realistic videos.Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, said on Friday that the platform would stop recommending "wholly AI-generated videos" in its popular Spotlight feed in favour of "authentic, human-made content."Over the past two weeks, YouTube, LinkedIn and Substack have unveiled similar strategies.Snap did not go so far as to try and prohibit all AI-generated content from Snapchat. The platform offers its own AI tools to alter content, and so AI "enhanced or edited" content will still be part of its recommendations to users.However, Snap acknowledged that entirely AI-generated content is typically "low-quality", "repetitive", and generally not what Snapchat users want to see.Recent research into the reception of AI-generated content shows that people tend to agree, external with those descriptions. Moreover, the more fake AI-generated content that people see in a social media feed, the less likely, external they are to think that any of the content they're being shown online is genuine, according to a separate survey.As Chris Best, the co-founder and chief executive of Substack put it last week: "It's getting harder to tell what's real on the internet."Announcing a new tool, external designed to let readers on the newsletter platform detect AI-generated writing, Best cited other research that has found up to 40% of writing on social media is now fake or AI-generated."Platforms that reward fakeness will create a race to the bottom," Best said.LinkedIn, a social media platform focused on work, introduced a button on its platform this week that allows any user to report if a post or a comment appears to be AI-generated."AI slop is a top priority for all of us," LinkedIn's chief product officer Hari Srinivasan wrote on the platform.In just the last couple of months, he said the platform had "blocked billions" of attempts to post AI-generated comments. "Every day we are now catching hundreds of thousands of automated comment attempts," Srinivasan said.Like Snap, LinkedIn said it is not rejecting the use of AI entirely and users that use AI tools to "refine" their posts should not get caught up in efforts to combat AI slop.Nonetheless, LinkedIn is removing an automated prompt that would show up for users writing a post offering to "enhance" it through the use of AI. It will go back to a simple proofreading tool.YouTube, the video platform owned by Google, also this month updated its policies, external around what kind of content can be monetised by creators.Research from last year found scores of channels on YouTube that were solely AI-generated content, external, many of which had millions of subscribers and some of which made millions of dollars in revenue.In an effort to discourage YouTube from filling up with what the platform calls "inauthentic content", earlier this month the site broke down into three categories the kind of videos that will not be allowed to make money through it: generic, repetitive, or template-based. Those styles of content are much easier to make, and quickly, with the use of generative AI tools.YouTube's trust and safety chief Matt Halprin said in an interview, external on the updated rules that, while AI tools can help people with their content, they are more frequently being used to create fake and low-quality videos."The same technology really enables great stuff," Halprin said."But it also enables stuff that's kind of content farming, and that's the stuff that we don't want to have."

schema.headline: Snapchat joins other platforms in the fight against 'AI slop'

title: What is Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and why does Trump say he wants to bomb it?
description: Image source, VantorByShayan Sardarizadeh, Jake Horton and Ghoncheh HabibiazadBBC Verify and BBC PersianUS President Donald Trump has repeatedly threa
body: Image source, VantorByShayan Sardarizadeh, Jake Horton and Ghoncheh HabibiazadBBC Verify and BBC PersianUS President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb a suspected underground nuclear site in Iran known as Pickaxe Mountain, where recent satellite images appear to show construction work taking place.Pickaxe Mountain is one of the few Iranian sites linked to the country's nuclear programme that has not been the target of US and Israeli strikes. There have been unproven claims that some of Iran's stock of highly enriched uranium may be kept there, which could be further enriched for use in nuclear weapons."We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily," Trump told reporters on 21 July. And on 28 July he said: "I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe. It's not a big problem - we took out their nuclear sites, and we'll have to take out Pickaxe if we don't make a deal."Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on 22 July that "no nuclear activity is taking place" at Pickaxe Mountain, and described US threats as "a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage".BBC Verify and BBC Persian have spoken to experts and analysed satellite imagery to piece together what we know about the site, and the potential impact of any strike.What do we know about Pickaxe Mountain?Kuh-e Kolang, which translates as Pickaxe Mountain, is located immediately south of the Natanz nuclear complex, Iran's largest uranium enrichment facility which has been bombed by both the US and Israel in 2025 and 2026.The site is believed to be buried deep inside the mountain and its exact purpose is shrouded in mystery and speculation.Tehran has previously indicated that it may be a replacement for a building within the Natanz complex used for the assembly of advanced centrifuges that was damaged after a suspected sabotage operation in July 2020.Former head of the Atomic Energy Organisation of Iran, Ali Akbar Salehi, said in September 2020, external that "a more modern, spacious, and comprehensive facility" would be built in the mountains "near Natanz", without naming Pickaxe Mountain.Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.The facility appears to have four tunnel entrances, two on the eastern side and two on the western end. Satellite images show that - over time - what appears to be a large perimeter fence has been built around the site, following the 12-day war between Israel and Iran in June 2025.Images captured on 30 June 2026 show several construction vehicles near one of the western entrances. And in recent months, satellite imagery indicate continued work on access roads and tunnel entrances around Pickaxe Mountain.According to analysis by the US-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS), external, Iran has partially filled the two eastern tunnels to block ground access."In the last year, we have observed fairly steady construction activity at the site," says Spencer Faragasso of the ISIS. "Iran's work there has likely centred around continued internal excavation and hardening of the facility that would provide further protection against aerial attacks."Could US bombing destroy Pickaxe Mountain?The site at Pickaxe Mountain may have been chosen to protect it from air strikes with some analysts estimating, external the core of the facility could be roughly 100m (328ft) underground.This would also mean it's buried deeper than Iran's two nuclear enrichment complexes at Fordo and Natanz which the US bombed last year using what are known as bunker buster bombs - the only known weapon that could conceivably reach such concealed sites.The US GBU-57 bomb weighs about 13,000kg (30,000lb) and is reported to able to penetrate 18m (60ft) of concrete or 61m (200ft) of earth before exploding.Iran’s secretive nuclear site that only a US bomb could hitIran fortifies underground complex near nuclear site, satellite images showBut even using these munitions, experts say the US would be unlikely to completely destroy Pickaxe Mountain."Obliterating every underground chamber would be extremely difficult because of the facility's depth and uncertain layout," says Arman Mahmoudian, a research fellow specialising in Iran at the University of South Florida.However, the US could target tunnel entrances, communications systems, access roads, and other supporting infrastructure, Mahmoudian adds, which "could paralyse the facility's operations even if some of its deepest underground sections survived".Meanwhile, Faragasso says the site may be potentially vulnerable and that "targeting the ventilation shafts would enable the weapons to reach deeper into the facility, and the tunnel portals can be collapsed using bunker buster weapons".What do we know about what's underground at Pickaxe Mountain?Information about exactly what is underground is not publicly known, and it is unclear whether the facility is operational.The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) - the global nuclear watchdog - has so far not been given access to Pickaxe Mountain by Tehran. Rafael Grossi, the director-general of the IAEA, said in March that Iran had "announced their intention to have nuclear activity there", external."This was part of their quite systematic intention to put their most sensitive facilities underground," Grossi added.The IAEA estimated in 2025, external that Iran holds roughly 440kg (970lbs) of 60% enriched uranium,There have been unproven claims that part or all this stockpile may be kept at Pickaxe Mountain, or that some of the undamaged centrifuges at Natanz or Fordo may have been transferred there, external after the bombings of both facilities."It is plausible that high value items, such as uranium gas centrifuges, were brought into and stored within the tunnels," says Faragasso. "We have seen lots of continuous and steady truck movement throughout the site, entering and exiting the tunnel portals, meaning it is possible that some of those vehicles had moved items inside."David Albright, the founder and President of the ISIS, says that the "concern is Pickaxe Mountain could be a location where Iran puts an enrichment plant that could produce weapon-grade uranium for nuclear weapons"."None of this is happening as far as we know, but the fear is that it could turn into a place to make weapon grade uranium metal," Albright adds.Tehran says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian use and denies any intention to develop nuclear weapons.Graphics by Tom Shiel.

schema.headline: What is Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and why does Trump say he wants to bomb it?

title: Women's Open: Haeran Ryu leads in pursuit of third straight major
description: AIG Women's Open-7 H Ryu (Kor); -6 S Kuwaki (Jpn); -5 Y Noh (US), A Thitikul (Tha); -3 S Joo (Kor); -2 L Woad (Eng), C Hull (Eng), C Wannasaen (Tha),
body: AIG Women's Open-7 H Ryu (Kor); -6 S Kuwaki (Jpn); -5 Y Noh (US), A Thitikul (Tha); -3 S Joo (Kor); -2 L Woad (Eng), C Hull (Eng), C Wannasaen (Tha), L Li (US), J Yan (US), L Coughlin (US), P Martin (Esp), M Katsu (Jpn)Selected others: -1 L Ko (NZ), N Korda (US), M Rhodes (Eng); +2 A Hewson (Eng), +6 G Hall (Eng), +7 M Yamashita (Jpn)Full leaderboardSouth Korea's Haeran Ryu birdied the 18th to bounce back from a poor start and end the second round as leader of the AIG Women's Open at Royal Lytham & St Annes.The 25-year-old, aiming to become only the fifth woman in history to claim three majors in a calendar year, is one shot clear of Japan's Shiho Kuwaki.Earlier this month, Ryu claimed her second major in the space of two weeks at the Evian Championship, and her remarkable major form has continued at the Open.Despite being three over for the day through five holes, she sank five birdies to shoot two under par and build on her opening-round score of 66."The last hole is so important as it is always good for tomorrow, I always want to make a good score on the last hole," Ryu told BBC Sport."I've had two birdies on it, which is a good thing."I just stayed patient after that [the tough start] and I made some birdies to finish under par. I am so happy now."Kuwaki, who finished Thursday two shots behind leader Jeeno Thitikul, carded a one-under-par round to take advantage of Thitikul's dropped shots.Following a spectacular seven-under-par 64, Thailand's Thitikul shot a two-over-par 73.American Yealimi Noh joins world number two Thitikul on five under par after shooting 70.England's Lottie Woad is in a strong position to compete for a first major title despite a disappointing end to her second round.The 22-year-old, who arrived as one of the favourites, ended the day on two under par.Woad's bogey-free opening round of 69 was followed up by a score of 71, which included three birdies on the front nine.However, two dropped shots on the back nine - one on 17 - leaves her five shots back.England's Charley Hull went round in even par to remain on two under par, while world number one Nelly Korda shot 68 to recover from an opening-round two-over-par 73.Three-time major champion Lydia Ko is also well placed to make a move from one under par, as is England's Mimi Rhodes, who recovered from two early bogeys to sink three birdies.Who are the best active players never to have won a major in the women's game?For many, Hull and Thitikul would be the first names that come to mind.Hull has finished runner-up in five majors, with her most recent near-miss coming in June's US Open.Her solid opening round at the Open left her two under par and in a strong position to challenge for a maiden major title.A tricky back nine on her second round ended in style, as a birdie from the bunker on the 17th was followed by a par at the last.It was not a round that ever truly caught fire, despite featuring three birdies, but it keeps Hull firmly in contention."I am really looking forward to it [the weekend], it's going to be loads of fun," Hull said."I feel like now my nerves have settled down. My back was actually playing up for me a little bit, a little bit sore, that's why I think I wasn't getting through the ball how I wanted to."Former world number one Thitikul, who has 11 top-10 finishes in majors, said the stronger wind compared with Thursday played a part in her scoring.She lipped out for birdie on the sixth and seventh before a lengthy par save on the 15th prevented back-to-back bogeys.Her faultless opening round contained no dropped shots, but that run ended on the third hole of her second round.Thitikul's only birdie of the day came on 12, but there could have been more. She also lipped out with her final putt, which would have pulled another shot back.Having spoken previously about struggling to cope with the noise of finally winning a major, Thitikul may be content for the spotlight to shift elsewhere after her stunning opening round.Following an opening two-over-par 73, Korda needed to hit the ground running in her second round to get back into contention.Korda's victory at the US Women's Open in June gave her a chance to complete the career Grand Slam, achieved by winning all five women's major titles.A run of four birdies in six holes began with a putt from about 20 feet on the fourth.Another lengthy putt from the edge of the green on the 11th continued what was becoming a sensational round."That's 36 [holes] in, 36 holes to go. You never know what's going to happen. It's golf. It's links golf," Korda said."I am just going to try to have the same attitude I had today going into the weekend."Having won the first two majors of the year, Korda is also in contention to become only the fifth woman in history to claim three majors in a calendar year.That looked unlikely after Thursday, but her performance on Friday showed why she is a four-time major champion with the chance to achieve something special.Her round still contained three bogeys and her last birdie came on 13, preventing a further climb up the leaderboard.

schema.headline: Women's Open: Haeran Ryu leads in pursuit of third straight major

title: Fifa World Cup plans: Gianni Infantino scraps private investment proposal after widespread opposition
description: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment planImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gianni Infantino has been the president of Fifa since Febr
body: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment planImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gianni Infantino has been the president of Fifa since February 2016ByJack SkeltonBBC Sport senior journalist and Simon StoneChief football news reporterUpdated 38 minutes agoFifa president Gianni Infantino says he has scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors following widespread opposition.Infantino said it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.The Swiss official added: "As a result, this proposal will not proceed."Infantino had offered Fifa's 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.However, Uefa - which governs European football - responded by voting to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead, and other governing bodies also voiced their opposition.On Friday, Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".That came after two other major confederations spoke out against the plans.Concacaf, which governs football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.It means Infantino is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March."Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve," the 56-year-old added in a statement."Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game."AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa welcomed the withdrawal of the plan."The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game," he said.Infantino's plans were unlikely to passDespite rejections from Uefa and Concacaf, Fifa initially vowed to continue with its proposals on Friday, saying "nobody is selling football".However, Infantino would have needed the backing of a majority of member associations to pass the plans - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour.That became unlikely when the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf in opposing the plans.Uefa has 55 votes, Concacaf has 35 and Asia has 46.If all member associations backed the stance of their governing body, that would have meant 136 nations voting against Infantino's plan.Governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) had said they would discuss Fifa's plan in August.Conmebol - South American football's governing body - said it had asked Fifa for "additional information and clarifications" regarding the "scope, structure, governance and possible effects" of the proposals.What was Infantino's plan?Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, with external investors able to buy stakes in it.It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).A 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan laid out how Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased payout of 24m euros (£20.5m) per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.It mentioned "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".There was no mention in the document of the women's game.Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time on Friday - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.Can Infantino survive?Figure caption, How does Fifa actually make decisions?Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat AFC president Sheikh Salman by 115 votes to 88. Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.Prior to this week, it had been anticipated Infantino would be re-elected unopposed. Associations around the world, including some in Europe, had already confirmed their intention to vote for him.It remains to be seen if the events of this week will result in a mass withdrawal of their support.In his statement, Infantino reiterated his plan was designed to strengthen member associations, "especially in countries where support is most needed" - but the proposal clearly created division within Fifa itself.Cordeiro, who represented Fifa on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup, is the first senior figure at the governing body to resign over the plans.In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value". He added he had no involvement in the proposal.It is understood Infantino even left some of Fifa's eight vice-presidents in the dark about his plan, which it is claimed could have raised $10bn (£7.5bn).Lamour called it "the project of one person" and said "a president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them" but this was "the opposite"."If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."'Bruised Infantino makes humiliating climbdown' - analysisByChief football news reporterAs reports first emerged on Tuesday about Fifa's plans, a senior figure in English football told me the story would be as big, if not bigger, than the European Super League.I do not think he felt it would unravel in quite the same way - but the idea only took two days longer than Super League to be scrapped.There have been no fan protests on the streets, but animosity towards the plans was evident from the moment the likely implications dawned on the game.Infantino is an astute politician. He knew the numbers were against him and has decided to cut his losses now rather than risk further personal damage.It is a humiliating moment - but for Infantino, the real work starts now. He has some significant bridge building to do.In their statement - which, in its own way, was just as damning as Uefa's threatened boycott - the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) pointed to a much wider issue. "The AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal," it read. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."Infantino cannot just walk away from the past few days as though nothing has happened. There are a lot of angry people in football who feel he has been acting beyond his power - just as the organisation's chief operating officer suggested on Friday.The immediate crisis has passed. Over the short to medium term, it will be fascinating to see whether Infantino can restore his reputation.TimelineMonday, 27 JulyIn a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account, Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells his critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership.Tuesday, 28 JulyThe Times and Financial Times report Infantino's plan to sell stakes in its competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors.Uefa publishes its first statement saying football is "not Fifa's to sell", and accuses Fifa of 'crossing a line'.Fifa issues statement confirming the plans.Wednesday, 29 JulyInfantino writes to all 211 Fifa member associations saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his plans, but must do so by 19 September if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).Uefa says Fifa "cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends".Thursday, 30 JulyUefa's 55 member associations vote to boycott World Cups if Infantino's plan goes ahead.Concacaf says its 41 member associations also "rejected" the proposal.Friday, 31 JulyFifa says "nobody is selling football" and vows to continue with the plan.Asian Football Confederation (AFC) says it "stands in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, though stops short of unequivocally rejecting Infantino's proposal.A senior adviser to Infantino, Carlos Cordeiro, resigns, citing "a bad deal for football" that would "mortgage football's future".UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Infantino is the "wrong man" to lead Fifa.Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour says the governing body's own administration has been "deceived" about the project.Saturday, 1 AugustInfantino releases statement at about 00:30 BST on Saturday, saying the plan will not proceed.

schema.headline: Fifa World Cup plans: Gianni Infantino scraps private investment proposal after widespread opposition

title: How police in US are using the power of podcasts to crack unsolved murders
description: Peter Chadwick had been on the run for nearly four years, charged with murdering his wife, when California police launched a podcast about the crime.H
body: Peter Chadwick had been on the run for nearly four years, charged with murdering his wife, when California police launched a podcast about the crime.He was captured in Mexico 10 months and 20 days later.Karen Schepers had been missing for more than four decades when another police force, in Illinois, debuted the first episode of a podcast last year about the cold case - and her body was found at the bottom of a river within weeks.Now Colorado investigators are hoping to bring in elusive tips about a 10-year-old unsolved murder, too. The Aurora Police Department (APD) released its own podcast this summer in an attempt to achieve justice for Chelsea Yasser, 21, who was found fatally stabbed in a shopping centre parking lot in 2016.As the barrelling behemoth of true crime content continues to flourish, police departments across the US and abroad are turning to podcast production for help solving cold murder cases and other investigations.Most departments don't have the staff, budget or time needed to produce podcast content, nor do they have the equipment or expertise.Others hold off for fear of repercussions, lawsuits and civil liability, says retired detective Alcazar.In California, Newport Beach Police Department's podcast about the fugitive Chadwick, for example, was not without controversy. The millionaire was introduced to viewers in Episode 1 as "a man who killed his wife in the peaceful coastal community of Newport Beach, California in October 2012".Chadwick had been charged and pleaded not guilty, but not tried - yet the podcast made no use of the word "alleged" and called the millionaire a "murderer". Critics argued that it flew in the face of innocent-before-proven-guilty parameters and that the job of police was to investigate, not adjudicate.The podcast was produced and hosted by public information officer Jennifer Manzella, who defended the choice at the time, saying police "put out the same kinds of statements all the time".She tells BBC News that she was trying to balance telling the story in an engaging way without jeopardising the investigation.After Chadwick's August 2019 apprehension, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison - where he remains.Houghton and Vartarian had just been assigned to Elgin's new cold case unit in 2024 when the chief informed them that the job would also involve podcasting."We're already starting this new unit," Houghton recalls. "Why are we adding something else new on top of that?"Houghton and his partner begrudgingly began figuring out how to arrange episodes and soon discovered the process was also helping them structure the investigation. They formed different theories about what had happened to the missing 23-year-old, and each theory naturally formed an episode.The podcast not only generated tips but also gave the detectives more ways to find leads. They started going through posts on social media about their own programme."They'd say, like, 'Oh, my mom worked with this person, or I live in this neighbourhood and I remember this.'"The detectives ultimately solved the case through old-fashioned policework; one of their theories had been that Schepers had crashed her car and ended up in the river.They had found a 1999 local newspaper story claiming that police had searched salvage yards by helicopter as well as dragging the Fox River but there was no evidence the latter had happened.  And they did not shy away from telling listeners this.So the department brought in a search company with the latest sonar technology as well as divers - and they found Schepers and her car at the bottom of the river in March 2025.Now they're on the third season of the podcast. They shook up the format for the second, focusing on homicides, but have returned to a missing persons case.Houghton acknowledges that "it is a lot of work - it takes a lot of time and effort".As other departments navigate those budgetary and resource issues, however, there's a consensus that podcasts as an investigative tool will be seen more frequently.If police departments can find the staffing to sustain it, podcasting could help in both recruitment and staff retention, says Janice Iwama, associate professor in American University's department of justice, law and criminology. It gives listeners the chance to learn more about what policing is really like, from the mouths of working officers.Generational change could also fuel the trend, says retired NYPD Detective Alcazar, because younger police officers will be more ready to embrace the opportunities presented by podcasts and social media."That's their world," he says. "That's what they're most comfortable with."

schema.headline: How police in US are using the power of podcasts to crack unsolved murders

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Georgia Hunter Bell eyes golden sweep after Glasgow win
description: Georgia Hunter Bell is eyeing an ambitious sweep of gold medals in 2026 after winning the 800m Commonwealth Games title in Glasgow.England's Hunter Be
body: Georgia Hunter Bell is eyeing an ambitious sweep of gold medals in 2026 after winning the 800m Commonwealth Games title in Glasgow.England's Hunter Bell dominated the field to add Commonwealth gold to the 1500m world indoor title she won earlier this year in Poland.The 32-year-old, a training partner of 800m Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, will also race at next month's European Championships and the inaugural Ultimate Championships in September."There are four opportunities to win gold this year," Hunter Bell told BBC Sport."I am two golds down and two more to go."Hunter Bell is blossoming later in her career. Having taken five years out from the sport before returning during the Covid-19 pandemic, she took 1500m bronze at the Paris Olympics before pipping Hodgkinson to silver at last year's World Championships in the 800m.This, though, is her first outdoor title - in the event Hodgkinson is Olympic champion."Every medal is a landmark moment but my first outdoor gold is huge," she said.Hunter Bell and Kenya's world champion Lilian Odira were the favourites for this title after Hodgkinson opted not to compete. The final was barely a contest with Hunter Bell setting the pace and then kicking on with 200m to go to win by more than a second.Hodgkinson has instead taken time off before the European Championships in Birmingham, which start on 10 August.Hunter Bell is only running in the 1500m in that event, denying the chance to see an intriguing race between the pair, but took her opportunity in her friend and training partner's absence. Though she said the win validates her decision to come to Glasgow, she defended the decision of others to withdraw.Dina Asher-Smith, Katarina Johnson-Thompson and Matt Hudson-Smith have been other high-profile English absentees."Every decision is different per athlete," Hunter Bell said."A few weeks ago I had to pull out of London which I was devastated about because I was sick. "We want to be healthy and racing at all times. "That is what people don't understand."If we could we would be racing non-stop. "We get incentivised financially, we love it. This is what we train for."If we are not showing up there was a reason for that."Later, Emily Newnham's late surge secured England silver in the 400m hurdles while Jake Minshull also took silver in the men’s race. Sammy Ball, the British under-20 decathlon record holder, and Lewis Church finished fourth and fifth respectively for England in the decathlon.

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Georgia Hunter Bell eyes golden sweep after Glasgow win

title: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record
description: This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown
body: This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown of a relationship from a female perspective, from Dean."[It's] very personal and reminded us of home, but when Olivia put her touch on it, it became a much more universal track," he told Radio 1, adding "that's what made it so huge and so beautiful".He said he wanted to "personally thank" Dean, who helped him achieve his first ever number one single, adding: "It wouldn't have happened without Olivia obviously, but now I feel like it belongs to the fans, they've made it what it is".When asked how he'd be celebrating the achievement, Fender joked "I think I'm just gonna have a really big sandwich".It hasn't been a straightforward ascent to the top for Rein Me In - originally released as a solo Fender track and repurposed as a duet in June 2025, it took eight months to reach number one in February this year.Dean said when the track came out, external that the original version of Rein Me In was her "favourite song on Sam's album" and  it was "a pleasure to write a new verse from a female perspective".A lot of the song's success as a duet comes from its authenticity, with the lyrics exploring the fallout from the end of a relationship and the difficulties faced by both parties as they try to move on from each other.Whilst Fender's verses feel full of anger and regret at not being able to open up and be the partner he wanted to be, they are complimented by the softer and more reflective tone of Dean's, in which she encourages him to try again to make it work.It has been described by Blunt Magazine's Jake Fitzpatrick, external as "stormy, tender and anthemic" and a "love letter to the kind of songwriting that knows when to burn slow".The song has also received praise amongst many critics and bloggers, including Cult Following's Ewan Gleadow, external, who says that Dean's addition helps it to find "a new depth", noting "charm is a big part of it too, with all those reflections on where you come from and where you're headed".Ben Mortimer, who runs Fender's label Polydor, described it as a "historic achievement" from "two homegrown stars" - Newcastle's Fender and London's Dean.In an interview with Radio 1 when the track first hit number one, Fender acknowledged the track's slow climb to the top, thanking "the internet".He also says he found it interesting that the track "travelled online and people came to it later, which is wonderful really because it's the music that's doing the talking".The song has become a mainstay on TikTok - a quick scroll through the social media app shows its use on everything from grand declarations of love to montages of holidays and even compilations of football goals and celebrations.It's also notable that the song first went viral after the pair performed it at a show at the London Stadium, home of Dean's team West Ham, in June last year.She then returned the favour a week later at Newcastle United's St James Park, performing the song this time at the home of Fender's footballing love.Whilst TikTok streams do not count towards the official charts, BBC research from last year explored how much of an effect the platform was having on what we listened to, particularly songs with meaningful and powerful lyrics.

schema.headline: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record

title: He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind
description: Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.But over the following two years
body: Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country. His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.Testosterone is a steroid hormone, which the body naturally produces. It drives physical development, builds muscle, and controls sex drive, primarily in males, but it also supports health in females. There is a synthetic version which doctors can prescribe, but which can cause liver damage, serious psychiatric effects and heart and respiratory problems if taken without medical oversight. It can also cause infertility in men and increase the risk of testicular cancer.The Paradigm Peptides case is the biggest to rock the industry, an unregulated market which has exploded into the mainstream over the past 18 months.Peptides are short chains of amino acids that our bodies produce and have long been used to treat medical conditions, including diabetes. More recently, they are being used in weight-loss drugs - GLP-1s. Another type of drug sold by Paradigm Peptides was SARMs - Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators - which target specific tissues to increase muscle and bone mass.Both these types of unregulated injectable drugs have become increasingly popular in the online wellness community - including among many young influencers.Social media is inundated with people extolling the virtues of various substances - such as BPC-157, GHK-CU and TB 500 - all of which purport to help build muscle mass, help with tissue recovery, or improve skin health. They are not licensed, can only be sold for testing purposes and are not suitable for human consumption.Three years ago, Murphy says he was in a good place. He was married to Laura, and they had built a "very stable, consistent, beautiful life" in the Smoky mountains in Knoxville, Tennessee.Murphy had lost 130 pounds (59kg) and had "completed a major health transformation" through diet and exercise."I wasn't into gym culture - I wasn't a big gym bro or anything," he explains. "But after I had lost all that weight, I wanted to start building muscle and these supplements seemed like a safe way of doing that."Murphy thought he was taking a daily dose of SARMs. Like peptides, they are not approved for human use and are seen as experimental drugs with a risk of serious liver damage, thrombosis and heart problems.Murphy says he felt safe taking them because they were clearly labelled a "dietary supplement" and Paradigm claimed it had a contract with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on various blogs, but this was not true."Like other victims, I trusted that the products were safe," he says. "They presented everything as research backed with claims of 99% purity - it was all a lie."Murphy started taking Paradigm's SARMs in January 2023. During the first few months, he says they seemed to be having a positive effect: he was able to do longer workouts and had more energy. Encouraged by fake research articles he had read on Paradigm Peptides's website, he then started taking other products too.Insomnia and mania began to set in - and that triggered him, he says, to "burn down" everything he had built - his marriage, his friendships, and his business.During the court proceedings, consultant psychiatrist and pharmacologist, Dr Erik Messamore, gave evidence to confirm that he believed Murphy had been suffering from a steroid-induced psychosis.As Murphy's life spun out of control, unknown to him, the FDA was already investigating Paradigm Peptides. It had been sending warning letters to the company since 2020 telling it to stop selling unapproved drugs. By September 2023, the FDA had seized SARMs products from Paradigm to carry out tests on them. It turned out, all the supplements had been mixed with testosterone.But it would take another six months before the FDA closed the business down.In the UK, Adam Taylor, professor of anatomy at Lancaster University, has been watching cases like this closely, as the scientific community continues to raise the alarm on this market which operates in a legal and regulatory middle zone. The products are not illegal to buy or own, but they are not approved for human use and so are not subject to the quality controls that govern pharmaceutical manufacturing."This might have happened in the US," Taylor says. "But consumers are at risk here in the UK, this is a global industry."He says a case like this demonstrates the magnitude of the risk, when "people think they are taking one product but it's actually something completely different"."So, they may also be getting additional side effects or different results that they can't explain."Murphy's wife Laura says her husband changed overnight. He had gone from a "loving partner" to a man who believed that she was "plotting" to take over his successful consulting business."One minute he would be crying and asking what was wrong with him, the next he would talk about wanting to take over Los Angeles," she says. "We had no history of mental illness in our family, Dan was so calm and stable before this happened."We did not know what to do."Life began to unravel. Murphy had an affair, was drinking copious amounts of alcohol, and felt his friends and family were out to get him - he even thought his mother-in-law wanted to murder him."I was in a full-blown psychosis - I believed that my loved ones were trying to hurt me and kill me," he recalls. "At this point, I've lost the plot. I'm not able to make any connection to the supplements, to anything that's happening."Then in December 2024, Murphy ran out of his supply of Paradigm Peptides supplements. It was then, he says, he felt his condition began to improve.Murphy and his family had no idea the FDA had been investigating the company, and it was not until February 2025 that he was told that the drugs he had been taking had been mixed with steroids."If only I had known, if the FDA had been more public, or even just put a notice on the Paradigm Peptides website. But instead, I'm taking this product and they know it's been cut with steroids," he says.So far, he says he seems to have made a full recovery. He is one of 167 of the victims who have come forward and sought a total of $78,317 (£58,169) compensation for the damage caused. Others had suffered blood clots, heart issues, anxiety and depression, the Department of Justice confirmed.Murphy says he realises now he was playing "Russian roulette" with his health and no longer takes supplements."Never again," he says, "and I'm speaking out now because I don't want people falling into the trap I fell into - that all supplements are safe. "I was gambling my health, my family and, in many respects, my life."

schema.headline: He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind

title: Ex-catering workers claim they are owed thousands in unpaid wages
description: Chrissy Bell is a senior advisor with Acas and spent 10 years working on its helpline. Acas provides free, impartial advice to employees and employers
body: Chrissy Bell is a senior advisor with Acas and spent 10 years working on its helpline. Acas provides free, impartial advice to employees and employers on workplace rights and disputes.  "If someone is expecting their wages on a certain date and it doesn't arrive or it doesn't arrive in full, then if people haven't got savings, even a small amount of difference can be the difference between them paying their bills and not being able to pay them," says Chrissy. She has this advice to anyone who believes they have not been paid the correct amount,"Firstly, work out the amount you should have been paid. So check payslips, timesheets, contracts and the first step is to speak to the employers, as there may have been a genuine mistake."If this does not work, she suggests putting a more formal grievance in writing, setting out any evidence, including timesheets, and then giving the employer a reasonable chance to respond.Finally, she says if it is not resolved internally after a reasonable amount of time then the person should consider making a claim to an employment tribunal if they are owed outstanding wages."If someone gets an award at an employment tribunal then there are systems in place to help them enforce it if necessary," she says. Martha Lindeque declined to provide a statement, but the BBC understands that her position is that she strongly denies the allegations made by her ex-staff.

schema.headline: Ex-catering workers claim they are owed thousands in unpaid wages

title: Same start but different outlook at Rangers era begins for McInnes
description: A year ago, Russell Martin tore strips off his Rangers team after an opening day draw at Motherwell.Two managers and plenty of disappointment later, i
body: A year ago, Russell Martin tore strips off his Rangers team after an opening day draw at Motherwell.Two managers and plenty of disappointment later, it was the same result but a different tone at Dundee United as the Derek McInnes era started in underwhelming fashion.The former Aberdeen, Kilmarnock and Hearts boss stressed the need for time and for further additions as he guides the Ibrox outfit through a summer of transition."It's one game," he told Sky Sports following a 1-1 draw on Friday. "I'm not really interested in what's happened previously, but from my point of view, we are going to get better as we go along."Having gone behind to Lachlan Rose's first-half effort, Rangers improved after the break and equalised through Thelo Aasgaard, but failed to capitalise and were fortunate not to concede late on when Jesse Randall dinked a tame effort straight at debutant goalkeeper Ivor Pandur."It's disappointing - we've dropped a couple of points, but we weren't good enough to get all three," McInnes added. "We've got to have more trust in what we're doing, keep our shoulder to the wheel and do simple things better."Former Rangers striker Steven Thompson agreed with McInnes that there is no need to panic."It's not the result Rangers wanted, but it is a point away from home at a difficult venue," he said on BBC Radio Scotland. "Other teams will come here and find it very difficult."At this point in the season, there's no knee-jerk [reaction] or anything here."It's not what McInnes wants, but it's the first game of the season. There will be time to judge once he gets the players he wants and once he gets more work done on the training ground."He will have learned a lot from his players tonight."On a night where Pandur, centre-back Ben Godfrey and former Hearts duo Cammy Devlin and Lawrence Shankland all made their debuts from the start, it was a glimpse into what this new-look Rangers side might look like under McInnes.Summer signings Dan Neil and Ross McCrorie also came on as substitutes and McInnes made it clear there will be further additions in the weeks to come.However, former Rangers man Andy Halliday saw what he believes to have been flaws in McInnes' tactical set-up."No matter how many defenders you play with, the main fundamental is being compact, and I thought Rangers were the furthest thing from compact," he said on Sportsound."All the best individuals, other than Thelo Aasgaard, were Dundee United players."Rangers are a work in progress, I think they'll still make additions to try and improve, but it certainly wasn't the start they were looking for."

schema.headline: Same start but different outlook at Rangers era begins for McInnes

title: CJP protest: India's 'Cockroach' protesters have wounds consistent with pellet-gun fire, experts say
description: Independent ballistic experts have told the BBC that injuries sustained by some Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters during last week's protest in t
body: Independent ballistic experts have told the BBC that injuries sustained by some Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters during last week's protest in the Indian capital were caused by pellet guns.Warning: This story contains images some might find distressingCentral Delhi witnessed overwhelming violence on 20 July when tens of thousands of protesters tried to march to the parliament to seek education reforms and the resignation of the education minister.Police and paramilitary personnel were seen brutally attacking the crowds with wooden sticks, batons and tear gas. Delhi Police said 60 protesters and 118 of their personnel were injured. CJP said the number of injured protesters was a lot higher than the official count.In the days following the crackdown, the government has not confirmed media reports that pellet guns were used on protesters.But the BBC has been able to confirm at least four cases where protesters have been treated at hospitals for wounds that experts say are caused by pellet guns.Pellet guns are shotguns designed for bird hunting. They fire cartridges, known as "birdshot", containing 200 to 400 small metal pellets. When used against crowds, the pellets spread out in a wide arc, striking people indiscriminately. These guns are banned in several countries.We have spoken to two of the injured men who believe they were hit by pellet guns fired by security forces. We have also shown photographs and videos of them and a third man to two independent armament and forensic experts. A senior official at a hospital has confirmed a fourth man who also received treatment for pellet wounds.The experts say the dozens of tiny round punctures are tell-tale signs of injuries caused by birdshot."The injuries depicted are definitely from a pellet gun," UK-based ballistics forensic scientist Philip Boyce told the BBC, adding that the weapon used is "a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun". "These pellet injuries can actually be quite devastating, especially at close range. The injuries I see [in Delhi] are not at close range, they're at least 50 feet. But they can actually still be devastating and potentially life-threatening even from 100 feet," he said.NR Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services (ARES) in UK, told the BBC that "images and video from the protests show the police using shotguns for crowd control" and photos of "injuries are strongly consistent with the use of birdshot"."While shotguns are a common tool in the less-lethal arsenals of many states, Indian law enforcement agencies have a long history of employing shotgun cartridges loaded with small lead pellets - known as 'birdshot' - in crowd-control scenarios. When loaded with birdshot cartridges, shotguns are sometimes referred to as 'pellet guns'," he added."But these pellets are not safe. They can result in life-changing or, occasionally, life-threatening injuries. They also pepper the body with toxic lead, which can sometimes be difficult to remove safely," he said.That's why many countries have either banned them or restricted their usage. In the UK, Boyce says pellet guns are widely used for shooting birds of prey and they're fairly freely available. But, he's "not aware" of any instance when they've been used for crowd control.In Indian-administered Kashmir - where pellet guns have been used since 2010 - official data,, external compiled by Human Rights Watch, shows they have injured several thousand people, killed at least 17 and blinded dozens. If it's confirmed that the forces used pellet guns in Delhi, this would be the first time that India would have used them on its citizens in its capital city.Two of the young men we spoke to told us they were injured in Connaught Place - a major hub near parliament - after 4pm local time on 20 July.Mohit (name changed) said when he saw a security personnel aim his gun at him, he turned around and began running in the opposite direction."Two-three seconds later, I felt a burning sensation on my right arm and back," the 28-year-old journalist told the BBC.Mohit said he kept running as a searing pain coursed through his body until he reached a café, bought a bottle of water and washed his wounds. "That's when I saw the tiny circular holes on my arm and upper back. I was completely freaked out." An X-ray taken at Safdarjung hospital, where he was treated for his wounds, shows tiny objects embedded in his arm and upper torso. Medical records that he has shared with the BBC show he has 26 pellet wounds on his right elbow and four on his upper right back. The notes include a diagram showing where the objects are lodged in his body.Mohit said the doctors told him that surgery could worsen his situation, but he worries about the damage "they can do in future since they remain lodged in my body or whether the ugly scars would ever go away"."But after seeing photos of other victims who've been hit in the face, I'm feeling fortunate," he says.Shaikh Irshad Mansoori, who works at a Gurugram-based firm, was not so fortunate.He was walking from Connaught Place to Jantar Mantar, the main CJP protest venue, when "the police and RAF [Rapid Action Force, a paramilitary force] personnel began beating the crowd with sticks and firing tear gas, causing a stampede-like situation and panic"."I was with a group of protesters and we were raising slogans when an RAF personnel pointed his gun at us. We didn't think he would fire, but then I suddenly heard a cracking sound nearby and pellets hit me on my left eyebrow and my chin."Some protesters tried to stem his bleeding with items of clothing, hailed a passing vehicle and took him to Lady Hardinge hospital.He said scans showed he had more than 40 pellets in his body, including three embedded deep in his neck, left eye muscle and under his nose that doctors told him needed to be taken out."Surgeons next morning removed seven pellets, but they had to leave the one in the neck as it was too risky to be taken out. They told me it's now part of your body. They've assured me that it would not cause any danger in future."More than 10 days later, Irshad says he's "still in some pain".A senior hospital official told the BBC that Irshad's injuries were caused by "pellet-type small particles", but would not say whether they were fired from a gun. "That's for the forensics to say once they've examined these pellets," they said.When the first claims of pellet gun use, external emerged last week, Delhi police, external called it "completely false and misleading". They said they did not even possess pellet guns. Since then, Indian media has reported that the shots were fired by the RAF, which reports to the paramilitary Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF). The BBC has reached out to CRPF chief Gyanendra Pratap Singh and also sent him questions on email. He's yet to respond.On Wednesday, government minister Jitendra Singh said in parliament that no "bullets" were fired, external and only tear gas was used. But he did not comment on the use of pellet guns.He was responding to allegations by Rahul Gandhi, Congress party MP and leader of the opposition in the lower house, who demanded that Home Minister Amit Shah be sacked since both the Delhi police and CRPF report to Shah.Last Saturday, Gandhi addressed a press conference accompanied by Sahil Lochab, a 19-year-old Delhi University student, who may lose an eye to pellet injuries. One side of Sahil's face and the back of his right arm are peppered with tiny holes. Gandhi lifted his T-shirt to reveal dozens more wounds on his underarm and body.In a video chat with Gandhi and in media interviews, Sahil said he supported the CJP protest, which centred around the issue of repeated paper leaks of key exams, because he wrote an exam to join the police force last year which was cancelled because of the same issue.He had gone to the protest with three friends but got separated in the chaos when police charged the crowd with batons. He was shot while marching towards the security forces with other protesters."I couldn't see who fired the pellet gun but it came from the side where the forces were," he said. "My right eye was swollen so much that it felt it had popped out of my face, I couldn't raise my right arm. I was bleeding profusely and some of the protesters took me to the hospital."His family, he told Gandhi, had tried to dissuade him from going to the protest, but "I couldn't stop myself"."I want justice. Whoever did this to me doesn't deserve to be in power," he said.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external Twitter, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: CJP protest: India's 'Cockroach' protesters have wounds consistent with pellet-gun fire, experts say
